candidates.name: Remember November 2026 (Polar Bear 2026)
aliases: This is a November meme from 2026, you won't understand yet
candidates.summary: A cursed AI polar bear that supposedly comes 'from November 2026' was revived in Sept 2026 singing 'Remember November 2026 is coming'. November 2026 is now four weeks away.
candidates.what: In 2023 an AI-generated image of a polar bear propped on its front paws spread on Russian TikTok with the caption 'This is a November meme from 2026, you won't understand yet'. It became a 'meme from the future' creepypasta. In late August 2026 a new AI video showed the bear singing 'Remember November 2026 is coming' to Oliver Tree's 'Life Goes On', and the format spread across TikTok and Instagram Reels in September. The joke is anticipation with no event at the end of it, so the meme's payoff is the calendar month itself.

origin.text: First posted on TikTok on 2023-03-27 by @gmd_arahis with a Russian caption (per search summaries of KYM content). English-language spread began September 2023. The current wave started with a late-August 2026 TikTok by @bigbakdiskk28 featuring the singing-bear video.

adopters.text: TikTok and Instagram Reels users, especially teen and young-adult meme audiences, making karaoke covers, edits of the bear next to a November 2026 calendar, and reaction skits. Explainer creators (YouTube, blogs) and creator-asset sellers are also cashing in.

spread.text: Independent coverage beyond the source platform: KYM database entries and a KYM editorial guide (syndicated to Yahoo US and Yahoo Singapore), plus separate explainers from meme.com, Neon Music, Cloutfluence and YouTube explainer videos. TikTok has topic pages for the phrase. The Yahoo copies count as one signal with the KYM guide.

trajectory.text: Revived late August, popularized in September 2026. A search summary says KYM recorded 980,000+ views within two weeks (unclear whether one video or an aggregate). No October-specific trajectory data was found. Inference: interest will probably spike again when November 2026 actually starts, then collapse after the month ends because the premise expires.

productDemand.text: Supply-side signals only. Etsy has market pages for 'Remember November 2026 shirt' and '...is coming'. TeePublic carries a 'Remember November 2026 is Coming Polar Bear Meme' long-sleeve. A YouTube Short promotes a tee. A Shopify store (Laima Design) wrote a content-marketing explainer. Creatorset sells a green-screen asset of the meme. No sales counts, reviews, 'sold out' reports, or press about people seeking merch were found. Listings show sellers expect demand, not that buyers exist.

competition.text: Several independent sellers already list shirts, long-sleeves, hoodies and totes on Etsy and TeePublic, and Redbubble shows at least one Polar Bear 2026 sticker among unrelated 2026 polar-bear designs. No November-2026 calendar wallpapers or printables appeared in the results, but this was a limited search, not a count.

gap.text: Most supply is apparel copying the AI bear or moody forest-and-moon graphics. Missing: (1) instant digital products that use the calendar payoff, such as a November 2026 phone wallpaper/lock-screen calendar with an original bear and day-by-day 'do you understand yet?' gags; (2) cheap stickers with a post-payoff punchline ('I remembered. November 2026.') that work for the whole month. Digital avoids POD shipping lag on a hard-dated joke.

window.estimate: Now through about 2026-11-30. Best selling days are likely late October to mid-November.
window.reasoning: The joke points at November 2026, and the month's arrival is a guaranteed attention trigger (inference). Digital products deliver instantly through November. POD orders placed after about Nov 15 arrive near or after month-end (1-2 week POD delivery). After November the premise is spent, though the 'meme from 2027' bird lore shows the 'meme from the future' format rolls forward to a new year, which is a different product.
invalidators: Attention already peaked in September and November passes quietly
Platform takedowns of listings that copy the AI bear image or reference the Oliver Tree song
A larger seller or brand floods the November moment
A real-world 'November 2026' event repurposes the phrase in a way that makes it unfunny or sensitive
window.seasonality: Hard-dated to November 2026. Overlaps early holiday shopping, so it competes for attention with Black Friday listings.

rights.note: Do NOT use the viral AI polar-bear image or video frames: who made it is unclear, and copying it invites takedowns. Do not reference Oliver Tree, the song title, or lyrics/melody. The phrase 'Remember November 2026 (is coming)' is a meme line with no known owner, and an original, clearly different polar-bear illustration plus text is low risk. 'Polar bear' and dates are generic. Risk drops to low if you use only the phrase and original art.

timing.rationale: Entry is possible only right now: about 8 weeks until the premise expires. Fine for digital, tight for POD shirts.

buyerIntent.rationale: Several independent sellers and a creator-asset vendor are monetizing, but no purchase evidence (sales, reviews, people asking where to buy) was found.

supplyGap.rationale: Apparel competition already exists on Etsy and TeePublic. The digital calendar/wallpaper niche looked open in a limited search.

productFit.rationale: Text plus one original illustration. A digital calendar wallpaper is a few hours of work with AI-assisted art and common design tools.

durability.rationale: Built-in expiry at the end of November 2026.

economics.rationale: Low price points (digital about $2-5, stickers about $3-5) and a sales window of a few weeks limit the upside. Search summaries put competitor tees at about $11-24, which squeezes POD apparel margins.

candidates.actionRationale: Test now, but only as a tiny, time-boxed experiment with low confidence. Spread is independent and documented, other sellers are already investing, the effort is a few hours, and the arrival of November is a predictable attention moment. Waiting means the window closes. Purchase evidence is still missing, so keep it to digital plus stickers, put no money into ads or apparel inventory, and stop hard by mid-November if nothing sells.

products.buyer: Teens and young adults (US) who follow the meme on TikTok/Reels and want to be 'in on it' on their lock screen during November
products.theme: 'November 2026: Do You Understand Yet?' phone wallpaper and lock-screen calendar pack. Original cartoon polar bear in a few poses (balanced on front paws, holding a calendar, shrugging on Nov 30), with day-by-day deadpan gag captions. Includes a printable desk-calendar PDF version.
products.whyBuy: Identity signal for the meme's own month; instant delivery; cheap impulse buy timed to the Nov 1 moment
products.differentiation: Uses the calendar payoff instead of copying the AI bear onto a shirt. Original art. Digital, so no shipping lag on a hard-dated joke.
products.validationTest: List on Gumroad and Etsy at about $3. Post 3-5 TikToks/Reels in the meme's format (bear reacting to the calendar) between Oct 25 and Nov 3, linking the product.
products.continueIf: 10 or more paid downloads, or clear 'where do I get this' comments, by Nov 4
products.pivotIf: Videos get views but no sales: offer it free as a lead magnet and test a paid sticker instead
products.stopIf: Fewer than 3 sales by Nov 10, or meme content volume visibly dies after Nov 1
products.rightsNote: No AI bear image, no Oliver Tree name/song/lyrics. Original bear art only.

products.buyer: Meme-literate teens and young adults decorating laptops, water bottles and phone cases
products.theme: Die-cut sticker of an original polar bear balancing on its front paws, captioned 'I remembered. November 2026.' (alt: 'Remember November 2026 - I still don't get it')
products.whyBuy: Cheap, giftable in-joke for the payoff month
products.differentiation: Post-payoff punchline that stays funny all through November, where competitors use the 'coming' framing that goes stale on Nov 1
products.validationTest: List 2 caption variants on Redbubble and as Etsy POD stickers by Oct 15, then compare favorites and sales.
products.pivotIf: Favorites but no sales: bundle as a free bonus with the wallpaper pack
products.stopIf: No sales by Nov 12 (POD delivery would then land after the joke expires)
products.rightsNote: Original bear only. Do not trace the AI image.

unresolved: No direct purchase evidence (sales, reviews, sold-out reports) was found for any Remember November product
Whether interest is still rising in October or peaked in September (no October trajectory data; search budget ran out)
How many competing listings exist (market pages seen, counts not visible)
Whether the Nov 1 'it's November 2026' moment actually produces a spike (inference only)

candidates.name: Kinda Chic trend ('kinda chic to...')
candidates.summary: A caption template where people call ordinary or hard-won things 'kinda chic', such as aging, body neutrality, sobriety or personal growth. Usually set in a butter-yellow font.
candidates.what: Creators overlay pale/butter-yellow text reading 'kinda chic to...' on a photo, video or carousel and finish it with something non-luxury they are quietly proud of ('kinda chic to be in your 50s', 'kinda chic to never stop learning'). It takes 'chic' away from money and gives it to aging, body positivity, mental health and small wins. Celebrities and brands picked it up in August 2026, and critics have called it a humblebrag.

origin.text: KYM dates early examples to April 2026, including an Instagram post by user mariabegins on 2026-04-27 about body positivity. It went viral July-August 2026.

adopters.text: Mostly women on Instagram and TikTok posting about body positivity, aging, mental health and personal growth. Celebrities joined (Drew Barrymore, 'kinda chic to be in your 50s'; Reese Witherspoon; Ashley Graham), and so did brands and businesses, including optical retailers covered by a trade publication. Search summaries say brands like Boots, Aldi and Virgin Atlantic used it, but the exact source page wasn't identified.

spread.text: Spread well beyond its origin: KYM entry plus editorial guide, US celebrity/lifestyle press (Hola US, syndicated to Yahoo; PureWow), UK business press (startups.co.uk September trends), a US alt-weekly (Riverfront Times), Spanish-language coverage (Emisoras Unidas, Sept 17), an optical trade outlet (Vision Monday), a Dictionary.com culture entry, and critical commentary (The Spectator). WhoWhatWear used the phrasing in an October 2026 shopping headline (per search summary).

trajectory.text: Built from April, surged July-August (celebrity and brand adoption in early August), still widely referenced in September and showing up in fashion copy in October. Backlash pieces ('humblebrag') usually appear near a trend's peak. Inference: likely at or just past peak as a meme, but the phrase may persist as an everyday template the way 'it's giving' did. No October search-interest data was available.

productDemand.text: Indirect only. Multiple Etsy sellers have launched 'kinda chic' apparel in niche variants (Kinda Chic to Be Kind sweatshirt; 'kinda chic' Comfort Colors tee; 'Kinda Chic to be Mommin'' hat; volleyball-mom sweatshirt; cheer-coach SVG files for crafters). Brands use it in marketing. No sales figures, reviews or reported consumer requests for merch were found.

competition.text: Etsy has a growing set of 'kinda chic' listings aimed at moms, coaches and sports parents, plus SVG files. Milestone-birthday, journal or planner products didn't appear in the limited results seen. Total listing counts weren't visible.

gap.text: The trend's most-shared emotional core is aging and self-acceptance (Drew Barrymore's 'kinda chic to be in your 50s'), yet the competition seen targets moms and sports parents. Missing angles: (1) milestone-birthday gifts ('kinda chic to be 40/50/60') as mugs and printable cards, an evergreen gift occasion that outlives the meme; (2) a 2027 'small wins' journal or planner with weekly 'kinda chic to...' prompts for New Year planner season; (3) a planner sticker sheet of everyday 'kinda chic' wins.

window.estimate: Holiday gifting and New Year planner season (Nov 2026 - Jan 2027); milestone-birthday designs possibly year-round if the phrase sticks
window.reasoning: It's past the August surge but still in active use in October. Birthday gifts and planners don't depend on the meme staying viral, only on the phrase still being recognizable. POD lead time (1-2 weeks) fits the holiday window if listings go up in October.
invalidators: The phrase becomes cringe because brands overuse it (backlash pieces already exist)
Fast fade in recognition before December
A trademark filing on 'kinda chic' for apparel (none found, not cleared)
Etsy niche fills quickly with milestone-birthday variants
window.seasonality: Peaked in summer 2026. Products ride holiday gifting, New Year planning, and milestone birthdays.

rights.note: Common words with no known owner. A web search found no 'kinda chic' trademark filing, but that's not a clearance (check USPTO before scaling). The butter-yellow typographic look isn't protectable. Don't use celebrity names, photos or quotes (e.g., Drew Barrymore). 'Kinda chic to be in your 50s' as generic text is fine without her name or image. Avoid health or body-outcome promises in journal copy.

timing.rationale: Past the August peak but still current, and holiday plus New Year demand windows are ahead.

buyerIntent.rationale: Seller proliferation and brand use suggest commercial interest, but there's no direct evidence of buyers purchasing.

supplyGap.rationale: Moderate competition concentrated in mom and sports niches. Milestone-birthday and journal angles weren't seen (limited search).

productFit.rationale: Pure typography in one recognizable color. Trivial to produce variants. A journal is a moderate lift with templates.

durability.rationale: A reusable template phrase with evergreen gift uses, offset by backlash and normal meme decay.

economics.rationale: Mugs and cards carry gift-level pricing on POD. Digital planners have near-zero marginal cost. Competition limits premium pricing.

candidates.actionRationale: Spread and identity value are well documented, and the phrase suits gifts and planners, but buying intent is still unproven and the meme is probably past peak. Prepare a differentiated holiday/New Year line (milestone-birthday mug and card, 2027 small-wins journal) and validate cheaply in October with one listing per format before expanding. Skip generic 'kinda chic' tees, which are already being copied.

products.whyBuy: Turns a dreaded milestone into a compliment using a phrase the recipient has seen everywhere this year. A ready-made gift.
products.differentiation: Aging/milestone angle, where the competition seen is mom and sports-parent apparel. The age series multiplies SEO entry points.
products.validationTest: Publish the 40, 50 and 60 versions as Etsy POD mugs and a $4 printable card bundle. Pin 6 mockups on Pinterest. Run for 3 weeks.
products.continueIf: Any age version gets 3+ sales or 30+ favorites within 3 weeks
products.pivotIf: Favorites without sales: shift to the cheaper printable card or a sticker
products.stopIf: Fewer than 10 favorites and no sales by early November

candidates.name: Jimothy the raccoon
candidates.summary: A round, short-spined wild raccoon in Seattle's Ballard neighborhood that went viral in July 2026 and turned into a local mascot and merch phenomenon.
candidates.what: Jimothy is a wild Seattle raccoon with an unusually short, rounded body (believed to be short spine syndrome) who scurries instead of walking. A resident's Instagram video named him 'Jimothy', went viral in July 2026, and made him a symbol of resilience and wholesomeness. He picked up Mariners tie-ins, an officially licensed bobblehead, a Google animation, a city 'Jimothy Summer' declaration, and a free Fortnite sidekick for Fortnitemares (Oct 1, 2026).

origin.text: Seattle resident Kiana Hall posted an Instagram video of the raccoon on 2026-07-14 and named him 'Jimothy' because 'he just looked like a Jimothy'.

adopters.text: A broad, wholesome-content audience. Seattle locals and Mariners fans (Salmon Run feature, card giveaway for Ballard Food Bank). Artists (fan art, tattoos, figurines, knit dolls). Faith and wellness writers framing him as a resilience symbol. Gamers and kids via Fortnite. Crypto speculators (a meme coin).

spread.text: Far beyond the original post: national press (Washington Post opinion, ABC/GMA, Today, The Hill syndicated to WGN), local TV (KOMO), legal press (Bloomberg Law, ABA Journal), e-commerce press (Fast Company, Shopifreaks), and gaming press (TheGamer, Vice) covering the Fortnite sidekick.

trajectory.text: Viral explosion in July 2026, then ongoing institutional tie-ins through August and September (Mariners, bobblehead, city proclamation) and an Oct 1 Fortnite sidekick that keeps him in youth culture. Inference: past the novelty peak but settled as a durable Seattle mascot. No September/October interest data was retrieved; the session search budget ran out before follow-up checks.

productDemand.text: The strongest merch evidence in this lens. Fast Company reported that Jimothy shirts, mugs, sticker packs and figurines took over Etsy and Amazon within about a week. An officially licensed bobblehead is on presale. The Mariners made special merchandise. A Yahoo headline reports a teenager turned a free raccoon baseball card into more than $20K (collectible resale). This is real buyer activity, though the card is an outlier.

competition.text: Saturated. Bootleg-style tees, mugs and stickers flooded Etsy and Amazon within a week of the video. Redbubble has a Jimothy shop page. An 'Official Jimothy Raccoon Store' sells Mariners-themed and 'Make Noise For Jimothy 2026' shirts. A licensed bobblehead exists. Slogans like 'In a world full of trash pandas, be a Jimothy' and 'if jimothy can i can' are already used.

gap.text: There's little room for generic Jimothy merch. The only plausible gap is a narrow Seattle-local holiday item (e.g., an original-art 'Saint Jimothy' ornament or holiday card for Seattle gift buyers), and even that is probably already contested.

window.estimate: Already mature. Holiday 2026 is the last obvious gifting moment.
window.reasoning: Merch supply has been flooding since July. The Fortnite tie-in sustains awareness among kids through October, but a new seller with no audience entering in October faces months of entrenched competition and weeks of discovery lag.
invalidators: News about the raccoon's health or death changes the tone
Someone (e.g., the original videographer) asserts trademark or copyright claims and triggers marketplace takedowns
window.seasonality: Summer 2026 peak ('Jimothy Summer'). Holiday gifting is a possible last wave.

rights.note: IP attorneys quoted by ABA Journal and Bloomberg Law say the name and a generic drawn image likely can't be trademarked, though Kiana Hall might have a claim (a high bar). The original video and photos are copyrighted, so don't trace them. Mariners logos and uniforms, the Fortnite sidekick design, and the licensed bobblehead design are off-limits. 'Official' store and licensing activity means takedown risk could grow.

timing.rationale: Entering about 3 months after a merch flood that began within a week of the video.

buyerIntent.rationale: Press reports describe a merch boom, licensed products are on presale, and a card resale is reported. Real but unquantified consumer purchasing.

supplyGap.rationale: Fast Company and Shopifreaks report Etsy and Amazon flooded, plus official and licensed products.

productFit.rationale: An original cartoon raccoon is easy, but avoiding photo-derived art and team or game IP takes care.

durability.rationale: Local-mascot status and the Fortnite tie-in help, but viral-animal interest usually decays and the subject is a wild animal with health issues.

economics.rationale: Heavy price competition from many bootleg sellers compresses POD margins.

candidates.actionRationale: Demand was real, but the market was flooded within days, licensed and 'official' products exist, and a new solo seller has no edge in October. Pass on general Jimothy merch. Revisit only if a new catalyst appears (e.g., a TV project, which The Hill hinted at) or for a narrow Seattle-local holiday item with original art.
